wstep: This card describes the NCHFP recipe for golden pepper jelly: yellow bell peppers and serrano chiles cooked in 5% vinegar, made into a jelly with sugar and liquid pectin and processed in a boiling-water bath.

sekcje.naglowek: Why you must not change the recipe
akapity: The FDA list gives peppers a pH of about 4.65–5.45.
Adding vinegar to the low-acid sweet and hot peppers is what makes this recipe safe for a boiling-water bath; do not reduce the amount of vinegar.
The amounts of vinegar and sugar are also needed for the pectin to form a gel.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): do not change the amounts of vinegar, peppers or sugar; the recipe is tested only in the proportions given.
White distilled vinegar and cider vinegar of 5% acidity are recommended for pickles.
Penn State Extension advises vinegar of 5–7% acidity for home food preservation and advises against diluting vinegar with water unless a research-tested recipe says so.

JarAtlas rule (cautious, for readers outside the USA): use white distilled (spirit) vinegar or cider vinegar labelled 5% or 6% acidity; do not use 10% vinegar and do not dilute it with water to make 5% vinegar; add only the water the recipe lists.
NCHFP uses US measures: a cup holds about 237 ml.

For about 5 half-pint jars NCHFP uses 5 cups of chopped yellow bell peppers (about 4 large, fleshy peppers), 1/2 cup of chopped serrano chiles (about 5 peppers), 1 1/2 cups of white distilled vinegar (5%), 5 cups of sugar and 1 pouch (3 ounces) of liquid pectin.
NCHFP allows sweet peppers of another color, which give the jelly a different color, and other hot peppers; JarAtlas rule: keep the amounts the same.
When handling or cutting hot peppers, wear plastic or rubber gloves and do not touch your face; without gloves, wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water before touching your face or eyes.
Wash all the peppers thoroughly and remove the stems and seeds; leave the membranes in the hot peppers, because that is where the heat is.
Put the sweet and hot peppers in a blender or food processor, add enough vinegar to purée them, and purée.
Put the purée and the remaining vinegar in an 8- to 10-quart saucepan, bring to a boil and boil for 10 minutes.
Remove from the heat and strain through a jelly bag into a bowl; several layers of cheesecloth can be used instead.
Measure 2 1/4 cups of the strained pepper and vinegar juice into the saucepan.
Stir in the sugar until it dissolves and bring back to a boil.
Add the pectin, bring to a full rolling boil and boil hard for 1 minute, stirring constantly.
Remove from the heat and skim off the foam quickly.
JarAtlas uses the optional NCHFP 10-minute process: the jars do not need to be pre-sterilized; wash and rinse them and keep them hot until filling.
NCHFP says this process may give a stronger vacuum in the jar.
Fill the hot jelly immediately into the hot half-pint jars, leaving 1/4 inch (about 0.6 cm) of headspace.
Wipe the jar rims with a damp clean paper towel, put on the lids and process in a boiling-water canner.
At 0–1000 ft (up to 300 m) process half-pint jars in a boiling-water bath for 10 minutes.
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased.
At 1001–6000 ft (above 300 m up to 1800 m) process them for 15 minutes.
Above 6000 ft (above 1800 m) process them for 20 minutes.
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m.
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage.
The NCHFP table gives times only for half-pint jars.
JarAtlas rule (NCHFP does not test metric jars): half a pint is about 236.6 ml, so a 0.25 l or 0.5 l jar has no tested time in this recipe; use jars of up to 236 ml, for example 0.2 l.
Let the processed jars cool undisturbed for 12 to 24 hours, then check that the lids have sealed.
Keep any jelly left over after filling the jars in the refrigerator.
Once you open a sealed jar, keep the jelly in the refrigerator.
Discard jelly with mold on it; USDA and microbiologists advise against scooping out the mold and eating the rest.
